chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Ziyad ibn al-Munthir, who said: I entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him).

And upon me was a pair of decorated socks (khuff), so he said: 'O Ziyad, what is this sock that I see upon you?' I said, 'A sock that I have taken.' So he said: 'Do you not know that the white [socks] are from the footwear, meaning the decorated ones, from the attire of the tyrants (jababirah), and they are the first to adopt it; and the red [socks] are from the attire of the Caesars, and they are the first to adopt it; and the black [socks] are from the attire of the Banu Hashim, and [it is] a Sunnah.'

key_terms.الْأَكَاسِرَة: The Caesars or Persian kings (historically associated with red attire)
key_terms.الْجَبَابِرَة: The tyrants or powerful rulers (historically associated with white attire)
key_terms.بَنِي هَاشِم: The clan of Hashim, to which the Prophet and Imams belong
key_terms.خُفٌّ: Leather sock or boot used for ritual wiping during ablution
key_terms.سُنَّة: A prophetic tradition or recommended practice
key_terms.مَقْشُورٌ: Decorated or peeled (referring to the texture/style of the leather)

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the color of socks in Shia jurisprudence according to Imam al-Baqir?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Baqir (AS) elucidates the socio-political symbolism of footwear colors, distinguishing between the attire of tyrants (*Jababira*) and Roman emperors (*Akasira*) versus the prophetic tradition of the Banu Hashim. This narration underscores the Shia emphasis on *Sunnah* as a marker of distinct identity and humility, contrasting royal ostentation with the modesty of the Ahl al-Bayt. It serves as a practical guide for believers to align their daily habits with the spiritual and historical legacy of the Imams.
